**The Weight of Words**

Words are strange things. They slip into the mind like smoke, curling around thoughts before we even realize they’re there. They can build bridges or burn them down. They can heal or wound. A single sentence can change the course of a life—yours or someone else’s.

I’ve always been fascinated by how words carry weight. Not just in the obvious ways—like a speech that moves a nation or a poem that lingers in the heart—but in the quiet, unseen ways. The way a parent’s voice softens when they say, *"I’m proud of you,"* or the way a lover’s tone shifts when they’re about to say something they don’t mean. Words are currency. They’re weapons. They’re lifelines.

Sometimes, I wonder if we underestimate their power. We throw them around like confetti—*"I love you," "It’s fine," "Whatever"*—without realizing that each one is a tiny act of creation or destruction. A *"no"* can close a door forever. A *"yes"* can open one you didn’t know existed. And silence? Silence is just another kind of word, heavy with everything unsaid.

I’ve spent years collecting words. Not in the way a hoarder collects things, but in the way a gardener tends soil—nurturing some, pulling weeds from others. There are words I’ve written that still haunt me, lines that felt true in the moment but now taste like ash. And there are others, buried deep, that I’ve never shared because they’re too raw, too fragile, too *mine*.

What’s the point of all this? Maybe there isn’t one. Maybe words are just echoes, bouncing off the walls of our lives until they fade into the static of existence. Or maybe they’re the only thing that makes existence bearable. A friend once told me that writing is just talking to yourself in a room where no one can hear you. But what if that’s not true? What if, in that room, you’re actually screaming into the void—and the void screams back?

I’ve been thinking a lot about loneliness lately. Not the dramatic kind—the kind that makes you want to scream into the sky—but the quiet kind. The kind that settles in when you realize no one will ever fully understand the way your mind works. Words are supposed to bridge that gap, but sometimes they widen it instead. You say something, expecting understanding, and instead get a blank stare. Or worse, a misunderstanding that twists your meaning into something ugly.

And then there’s the opposite—the way words can make you feel *seen*. A text from a friend at 3 AM, a poem that mirrors your soul, a stranger’s words that make you feel less alone. Those moments are like finding a door you didn’t know was there, and walking through it into a room you didn’t know existed.

I wonder if language is a kind of magic. Not the flashy, wand-waving kind, but the slow, insidious kind—the kind that rewires your brain without you noticing. The way a word you hated as a child becomes beautiful when you hear it in a song. The way a phrase you’ve heard a thousand times suddenly makes sense when you’re heartbroken. Words change. They evolve. They betray us. They save us.

I’ve been writing this for a while now, and I still don’t know what I’m trying to say. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe the act of putting words down is more important than the words themselves. Maybe it’s just about the weight of trying.

Because here’s the thing about words—they’re never just words. They’re the shape of our thoughts. They’re the ghosts of conversations we’ll never have. They’re the only proof we have that we existed at all.

So I’ll keep writing. Even when it feels pointless. Even when it feels like shouting into the dark. Because what else is there to do? Words are all we have.

And sometimes, that’s enough.
